newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Burger chain seen dampening GIB profits.
newsitem.headline: Burger chain seen dampening GIB profits.

text.p: Losses at fast-food chain Quick are seen dampening the profit rise of its parent company Belgian retailer GIB Group and countering the cost savings from GIB's supermarket restructuring, analysts said.

Consequently, several considered GIB's shares too expensive. "Investors are focusing on quality and visibility. We have GIB on a "hold" rating - there's a lot of uncertainty in the results," said Thierry Masset, analyst at Vermeulen Raemdonck.
GIB is due to publish first-half results after market hours on Thursday.
Masset calculated GIB's price to 1997 earnings ratio at 17, the same as Delhaize and versus 18.5 for Colruyt.

He expected GIB, Belgium's second largest retail group after Delhaize in terms of consolidated turnover, to announce a group net current profit - that is before any exceptionals - of between 750 and 850 million francs.
GIB made a group net profit of 645 million francs in the first half of 1995.

For full year 1995, GIB had a consolidated turnover of 228 billion francs. It fell into the red with a group loss of 4.6 billion francs after losing 4.1 billion francs on the sale of U.S. home-improvement chain DIY Handy Andy and writing off 1.7 billion on assets relating to its other U.S. unit Scotty's.
Quick, 57.44-percent owned by GIB, said last month the scare over "mad cow" disease in Britain sent first-half 1996 group net profit plunging to seven from 147 million a year earlier.
In full year 1995, restaurants and fast foods acounted for eight percent of GIB's consolidated turnover but 39 percent of operating profits.

Masset said weighing on first half results with Quick Restaurant's disappointing performance would be poor weather in March, April and May which was likely to have affected sales at GIB's European home-improvement stores.

Analysts said ongoing restructuring at GB supermarkets was expected to show further reduction in the company's cost base, but it remained to be seen how much of the saving had been passed on to customers through price cutting. Super- and hypermarkets together account for 63 percent of total sales.
Maud Watelet at Mignon, Hanart, Declerck cautiously forecast a rise in first half current group net profit of 10 or 11 percent, adding GIB's strategy for the medium term was unclear.
Caroline Lauwers at Bank Degroof was more optimistic and estimated group net profit in the region of one billion francs.
She was expecting a better performance from the supermarket sector of the group and did not consider the stock too dear.
"We're on "hold", but I might recommend "buy" if this year shows signs of a turnaround for GIB," she added.

Capital gains totalling 2.48 billion francs from the recent sale of GIB's stake in Sodal, the operator in Belgium of French hi-fi, photo and multi-media chain FNAC, and of its 25 percent interest in U.K.-based DIY chain Homebase, were expected to figure in its second half 1996 accounts.

One analyst said possible further divestments could be the performing units in the speciality division like Pearle Vision Center or Club, or - in the same sector - clothing retailer Sarma and department stores Inno. With the latter GIB would first try to eliminate losses, he said.
GIB has already said it is looking for a partner for Inno to boost buying power.

GIB shares have traced a roller coaster ride over the last five years on the Brussels bourse, hitting a closing high of 1,660 francs in March 1994, then falling to 1,136 by October 1995 when the loss on the Handy Andy sale was announced.
By March this year GIB shares had risen to 1,550 but then slid again, closing at 1,302 francs on Tuesday.
